sections.body_en:
Purification is accomplished through tevila (immersion) in a mikva (ritual bath), and the mitzva of tevila is that the entire body be within the water, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:16): "He shall bathe all his flesh in water." The Sages learned from the word "et" (אֶת) that together with the body one must also immerse all the hair attached to the body (Eruvin 4b). If she immersed and left even one finger or one hair outside the water, her tevila is invalid. Nor will it help for her to immerse that same finger or hair again; rather, she must go back and immerse her entire body in the water together with every hair at once. Even if many years have passed since she became impure, and in the meantime she has washed herself every day in a shower or a bath, as long as she has not immersed in a mikva she remains in her impurity, and all intimacy between her and her husband is forbidden by Torah law (Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 4:3; SA YD 197:1).

As we have learned (above 1:12), it is through water that God bestows life upon all His creatures; therefore water alludes to the supernal kindness, and when the waters are gathered together in a mikva they express the idea of unity that is revealed in Knesset Yisrael (the collective soul of the Jewish people). It follows that she who immerses in the water absorbs herself into the supernal kindness and becomes included in the holiness of Knesset Yisrael, and as a result, when she comes up out of the water she is as if born anew and purified. Accordingly, it is understandable that only when the entire body, including the hair, is immersed within the water is it absorbed and included in the source of its life and renewed. The difference between immersing the whole body and hair in the water and immersing the body when one finger or one hair remains outside the water is like the difference between a finite number and infinity: however large the number may be, the difference between it and infinity is abysmal, infinite.

In addition to the requirement that the whole body and the hair be within the water, there must also be no ḥatzitza (interposition) upon them, such as glue or dough, which prevents the water from coming into contact with the body or the hair. One may say that a spiritual idea can be learned from this halakha: it is not enough for the woman immersing to connect herself in a general way to the source of her life; rather, the connection must include all her traits, talents and desires without interposition, so that all of them will be bound to the supernal kindness and renewed. Therefore she must immerse without clothing and without any interposition, as will be explained below.

A ḥatzitza is something adhering to the body or the hair that prevents the water from coming into contact with them. By Torah law, an interposition invalidates only under two conditions:
(a) That it be on most of the body or most of the hair. (b) That one is particular to remove it. The Sages added a fence around the Torah and decreed that even if only one condition is fulfilled, it interposes. That is, even if there was an interposition on most of the body or most of the hair that one is not particular to remove, it interposes. Likewise, if there was an interposition on any small part of the body or the hair that one is particular to remove, it interposes. Therefore glue, honey, excrement, hard mud, the discharge at the corner of the eye and the like that have stuck to the body or the hair, even on a small spot, interpose, since one is particular to remove them (Mishna Mikva'ot 9:2; SA 198:7, 12-16).

But an interposition on a small part of the body that the woman immersing is not particular to remove, and that most women are also not particular to remove, does not interpose, since it is subordinate to the body. Therefore eye makeup, and nail polish or a nail build-up (artificial nail) on the fingernails, since women do not want to remove them but on the contrary want them to remain, as long as they are well done, are subordinate to the body and do not interpose. But if they have become damaged to the point that one usually removes them, they are not subordinate to the body and they interpose (Eruvin 4b; Nidda 67b; SA 198:1, 8, 17. On makeup and nails, see below, sections 12-13).

An interposition that women sometimes want to remove is not subordinate to the body and interposes. Therefore a garment or a piece of jewelry that is tight against the body, so that the water does not get under it, interposes, since women sometimes want to remove them so that they will not get dirty. And if they are not tight against the body, they do not interpose, since the water gets under them (SA 198:1-2, 23).

A ring that is tight on the finger, so that the water does not get under it, does not interpose if one is not particular to remove it at certain times. But a ring that women are sometimes particular to remove, such as a ring with engravings that women usually remove while kneading so that dough will not get into its engravings, interposes (below, n. 13). And if the ring is not tight, since the water passes under it, it does not interpose in any case. Similarly, earrings and nose rings that are fastened tightly to the body do not interpose if there is no time at which the woman immersing is particular to remove them; and if there is a time at which she is particular to remove them, they interpose (SA 198:23; Gan Ha-melekh 123).

All this is according to the strict law; however, ideally (lekhatḥila) the custom of righteous women is to be meticulous and remove every garment, every piece of jewelry and all makeup for the tevila (Rema 198:1). Only when there is a particular need do they act according to the strict law. For example, when a woman wishes to wear makeup and the tevila is on Friday night, she may immerse with long-lasting makeup, since by law the makeup does not interpose (below, section 12). Similarly, when a woman is compelled to immerse in the sea and is apprehensive about removing her clothes, she may immerse with a loose garment that the water gets under. And if she has a tight-fitting swimsuit, after she enters the sea she should lift every part of it so that the area beneath it gets wet; then, even after the garment returns to its place, she may immerse with it, since the sea water will join with the moisture beneath the garment and surround her entire body as one.

These are the main laws of interpositions; the details of the laws in various questions and special cases will be explained at the end of the chapter, in sections 12-16.1

notes_en.en:
The laws of interposition apply to all the immersions in the Torah, for both men and women; but since the Temple was destroyed, the Torah mitzva of tevila is fulfilled by women (and by men who ascend the Temple Mount). According to the Rambam, being particular is determined according to the opinion of the woman immersing, and according to the Rashba, according to the opinion of most women in that place and time. In practice, the ruling is stringent in accordance with both views (SA 198:1; Baḥ 1; Taz 3; Shakh 2. Below, at the end of section 12, the law regarding those who work with paint and are not particular about paint stains will be explained).
An interposition that one is particular to remove means one that one is particular not to go out into the street with. But an interposition that one is not particular to remove in the street, and only at times, such as before Shabbat or a wedding, is one particular to remove it, does not interpose (Kovetz Teshuvot 3:127; Masoret Moshe vol. 2, p. 223). These principles will be explained at length below in sections 12-16.
The Rema wrote (198:1): "Ideally she should not immerse even with things that do not interpose, as a decree on account of things that do interpose." Some hold that according to the Rema one must remove makeup and everything else even when, according to the rules of halakha, it does not interpose, and accordingly those of Ashkenazic descent who follow the Rema must act so (Piskei Mishna, Hilkhot 11:1; Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv in Mishmeret Ha-tahara 198:12). However, the Rema's intent is that it is a pious custom (minhag ḥasidut) to remove every interposition, but he too agrees that in a time of need one may ideally act according to the halakha, for the Sages said (Nidda 67b) that one should not forbid a minority that is not particular, because one does not enact a decree upon a decree. So too wrote Arukh Ha-shulḥan 198:9; Sidrei Tahara 198:6.

sections.body_en:
Although the entire body must be within the water all at once, there is no obligation for the water of the mikva to come into contact with every part of the body, but only with the exposed parts of the body, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:13): "He shall bathe his flesh in water", his flesh that is visible to the eye (Kiddushin 25a). But the places that are sometimes exposed and sometimes hidden, which are called "beit ha-setarim" (hidden places) and "beit ha-kematim" (places of folds), need not come into contact with the water of the mikva. However, there must be no interposition in them (Mishna Mikva'ot 8:5; Nidda 66b; SA 198:24-25). That is, on the one hand, since "beit ha-setarim" and "beit ha-kematim" are naturally exposed at times, there must be no interposition in them, so that if they are exposed the water will be able to come into contact with them. On the other hand, since in a natural position they are sometimes hidden, there is no obligation that they come into contact with the water.

An example of "beit ha-setarim" is the cavity of the mouth: when the mouth is closed, the water will not enter it, and if the one immersing opens his mouth, water will enter his mouth. Likewise the cavity of the nose: when the one immersing stands, the water will not enter it, but if he immerses with his face turned upward, the water will enter it. An example of "beit ha-kematim" is the armpit. When the arms are close to the body, folds of flesh form that the water does not enter, and the further the arms move away from the body, the folds open and the water can come into contact with them. And with heavier people, only if they open their arms wider will the water enter all the folds. And with very heavy people, even then folds of flesh will remain covered.

To summarize, there are three kinds of parts in the body: (a) The exposed parts must come into contact with the water, and an interposition on them invalidates. (b) "Beit ha-setarim" and "beit ha-kematim", which are sometimes exposed and sometimes hidden: as long as they are naturally hidden, they need not come into contact with the water, but an interposition in them invalidates. (c) "Internal places" (mekomot belu'im), such as the throat and the rectum, need not come into contact with the water, and an interposition in them does not invalidate either. Likewise the inner parts of the cavity of the ear and the cavity of the nose, as long as they are not visible from the outside, are called "internal places"; an interposition in them does not invalidate and there is no need to clean them.

sections.title_en: Preparations for Tevila: The Enactment of Ezra
sections.body_en:
Ezra the Scribe enacted that the woman immersing wash her hair and comb it before her tevila, in order to ensure that her tevila will be valid, without interposition. That is, by Torah law it is enough for the woman immersing to look over her body and feel her hair and the places on her body that she cannot see, so that she will know that there is no interposition on them. However, since not every woman is able to check her hair properly, Ezra enacted that the woman immersing wash her hair in water to remove dirt from it, and comb it to undo the knots in it (Bava Kamma 82a). The washing of the hair (ḥafifa) should ideally be in hot water, which helps remove the dirt and eases the undoing of knots and the combing of the hair, and not in cold water, which may harden the oil on the hair and cause the hair to tangle and form knots (Nidda 66b; SA and Rema 199:2).

As a continuation of Ezra's enactment, the Sages instructed that the woman immersing rinse the covered and hidden places on her body where dirt may accumulate, such as the armpits, between the legs, between the toes, the navel, and the other places that have folds. She should also clean her nose, ears and mouth, and brush her teeth (Nidda 66b). The general rule is that she should wash her whole body in hot water, with emphasis on the covered and hidden places, as women usually wash when they wash thoroughly (SA 199:1).

A woman who usually cuts her nails should be careful to cut them before the tevila. A woman who wants to grow her nails should clean them well, because the dirt under them interposes. And if there is polish on them, she should make sure it is intact (below, section 12). Likewise, it is preferable that before the tevila she remove hair that women usually remove for the sake of beauty. Admittedly, there is no concern of interposition with this hair, since it is attached to the body; however, from the standpoint of the mitzva of ona (marital relations), every adornment with which a woman adorns herself in preparation for the tevila is included in the preparations for the Torah mitzva of simḥat ona (bringing joy in marital relations) (Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 2:5).

If she immersed without examining her body, or without washing and combing her hair, her tevila is invalid. And even if she examined herself after the tevila and found nothing interposing on her body and no knot in her hair, her tevila is invalid, for perhaps there was something at the time of the tevila and it fell off or came undone after she came up from the tevila (SA 199:8). But if she immersed after washing her hair and examining her body, without having washed her body and without having cleaned the hidden places of her body, as long as she does not know that there was an interposition there, her tevila is valid.2

notes_en.en:
By Torah law, one must look over the body and feel the hair in order to know that there is no interposition, and after the examination one may immerse. Ezra the Scribe added an enactment that every woman wash her head, as explained above (Bava Kamma 82a), and the Sages further instructed to clean beit ha-setarim and beit ha-kematim (Nidda 66b). In addition, the Rishonim wrote that it is proper to rinse the entire body in hot water (Ramban, Rashba, Ran and others). And some say that rinsing the entire body in hot water is included in Ezra's enactment (Rabbi Shemarya in the name of Rashi; Ra'avan).
If after her tevila she found an interposition in her hidden places, such as a piece of meat between her teeth, her tevila is invalid. But if it is possible that the interposition came from meat she ate after the tevila, we presume that the interposition got stuck in her teeth after the tevila, and her tevila is valid (SA 199:9, 12). This is because according to many, the requirement that beit ha-setarim and beit ha-kematim be fit for the water to reach them is rabbinic (Ramban, Ritva and Mishneh La-melekh), and therefore in a case of doubt one should be lenient (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 198:56). And some say that by Torah law beit ha-setarim and beit ha-kematim must be fit for the water to reach them (Tosafot and Meiri, Kiddushin 25a); nevertheless, even according to them their law is more lenient, since there is no need for the water of the mikva to come into contact with them (see Shakh 198:32).

sections.body_en:
The ideal position for immersion is with the knees bent and leaning forward, with the legs slightly apart and the arms slightly away from the body, for this is the position in which most of the folds of flesh ("beit ha-kematim") open up and come into contact with the water. Not standing fully upright, a position in which folds sometimes form under the chest and between the buttocks and the legs, and not bending too deeply, which creates folds in the abdomen. Some are stringent and hold that if she immersed upright or very bent over, even if she did not contract her limbs forcefully, since the water did not reach the folds that formed in her body, her tevila is invalid. However, in practice, even if she immersed upright or very bent over, and folds of flesh formed in her body that the water did not reach, since she immersed in one of her natural positions, her tevila is valid (SA 198:35).

But if she forcefully contracted one of her limbs, for example if she immersed with her hand tightly clenched, or pressed her lips together tightly, or immersed with her arms or legs pressed tightly against her body, since this is not one of her natural positions and the water did not reach the contracted place, her tevila is invalid (Mishna Mikva'ot 8:5; SA 198:27, 38-39).

If her limbs were wetted with the mikva water before she clenched her hand, or pressed her lips together tightly, or pressed her arms or legs together, then even according to the stringent view her tevila is valid. This is because her contracted limbs remained wet, and thus the mikva water came into contact with all parts of her flesh, including those that were contracted (Rambam, Hilkhot Mikva'ot 1:9; Taz 198:27). For this reason the woman immersing need not lift her feet off the floor of the mikva during the tevila, for since the soles of her feet were wetted first, even when they are on the floor the mikva water joins the moisture on them and thereby surrounds all of her (SA 198:30).

Since wetting the body with the mikva water serves to remove all doubt even according to the stringent view, it is proper to immerse twice, to ensure that in the second immersion the whole body, including its folds, comes into contact with the mikva water.3

notes_en.en:
Mishna Mikva'ot 8:5: "If she clenched her hand or pressed her lips together, it is as if she did not immerse", since the water did not enter the place where the hand or lips were contracted. Nidda 67a: "Rabbi Yoḥanan said: If she opened her eyes too wide or shut her eyes too tightly, the tevila does not count for her." Many have the reading in the Gemara that with regard to tevila for her husband, the halakha does not follow this statement, because Rabbi Yoḥanan is stringent even when the water did not touch the body because of a position considered natural, whereas the halakha is as explained in the Mishna, that only when the water did not come into contact with part of the body because of an unnatural contraction is the tevila invalid (Ramban, Rashba, Ran and others). And some say that the halakha follows Rabbi Yoḥanan, since he too is speaking of an unnatural contraction, and his words are like the words of the Mishna (Rashi).
Also in Nidda 67a: "Reish Lakish said: A woman should immerse only in the manner in which she grows." Rashi: "That is, she should not press her arms against her flesh, nor her legs and thighs against each other, but rather in the manner of her ordinary walking and activity." So too wrote Rid, Riaz, Or Zaru'a, Rosh and others. According to the Ra'avad, the halakha follows Reish Lakish, and the meaning is that she should not immerse very upright or very bent over, and if she immersed so, her tevila is invalid. His words are cited in SA 198:35 as the view of "there is one who says", and this is the Baḥ's opinion in practice. However, according to the unattributed ruling of the SA, and likewise the opinion of nearly all the Rishonim, any position is valid provided that she does not contract one of her limbs in an unnatural way, and Reish Lakish's guidance is an ideal (lekhatḥila) (Arukh Ha-shulḥan 198:84). In any event, according to all opinions, if the contracted place was first wetted with the mikva water, her tevila is valid (Taz 198:38; Sidrei Tahara 198:55, and many others. And see Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 31, n. 5).

sections.body_en:
Since immersion for purity is a mitzva, the Sages enacted that the woman immersing recite the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us concerning immersion." Even when she became forbidden to her husband because of a stringent custom accepted throughout Israel, since in practice, according to the halakha, the couple were forbidden, she should recite the blessing over her tevila. But if according to the rules of halakha the woman was pure, and in order to satisfy all the poskim it was agreed by the rabbi and the couple to be stringent, then since by the essential law the woman is pure, she should not recite the blessing over her tevila.4

Customs differ regarding the time of the blessing. Some say that, as with all mitzvot, one must recite the blessing before performing the mitzva. It is preferable that she say the blessing in a respectful manner while dressed in a robe or wrapped in a towel, and immediately afterward enter the mikva and immerse (Rambam and SA 200:1). This is the custom of some women of the communities of the East and North Africa.

And some say that the correct custom is to recite the blessing after the tevila: since converts recite the blessing after the immersion, because before the immersion they are not yet Jews, the Sages established that all who immerse should recite the blessing after the immersion. In addition, since the woman is about to become pure, it is preferable to honor the blessing and say it in purity. In practice, according to this custom, women are meticulous to immerse twice and recite the blessing between the two immersions, and thereby satisfy both views, for they recite the blessing after the first immersion and before the second immersion. This is the custom of all women of Ashkenazic descent and most women descended from the lands of the East and North Africa. And each woman should continue her mother's custom.

According to the custom of reciting the blessing in the water, many women are meticulous to hug their bodies with their arms below the heart or over the heart, in order to separate between the heart and the private parts while reciting the blessing. In addition, although women are permitted to recite blessings without a head covering, some are meticulous to cover their heads while reciting the blessing, and some ask the balanit (mikva attendant) for this purpose to place the edge of a towel on their heads during the blessing.5

notes_en.en: The Dagul Mervava wrote that a woman who immerses because she became forbidden through "dam tohar" (blood of purity after childbirth; below 9:8) should not recite the blessing, for how can she say "and commanded us" regarding something that even the Sages did not decree, and which is only a custom. So too wrote Leḥem Ve-simla 194:4, and Taharat Ha-bayit 11:3. However, the opinion of most poskim, and likewise the custom of most Jewish women, is to recite the blessing over this tevila too. There are several reasons for this, the main one being that since the poskim equated the laws of "dam tohar" with the other kinds of blood, the law of tevila must be equated as well. Furthermore, since the custom forbidding "dam tohar" was accepted throughout Israel, violating it involves the prohibition of "do not forsake [the teaching of your mother]", and consequently the tevila is a full obligation (Ḥatam Sofer YD 191; Rabbi Shlomo Kluger; Tiferet Tzvi 19; Darkhei Tahara 11:14, in the note; Or Le-Tziyon vol. 4, 42:9; Badei Ha-shulḥan 194:24). But if according to the halakha it would have been possible to be lenient, and in order to satisfy all the poskim it was agreed by the rabbi and the couple to be stringent, she should not recite the blessing over her tevila. Similar to this was written in Ḥut Shani 200:1; Shi'urei Shevet Ha-levi 200:10.

Pesaḥim 7b: "Rav Yehuda said in the name of Shmuel: For all the mitzvot one recites the blessing before performing them... Rav Ḥisda said: Except for immersion alone", because "the man is not yet fit." According to the Rif, Rambam, Ra'avad, Rabbenu Tam, Rokeaḥ, Rosh and Or Zaru'a, only a convert immersing for his conversion recites the blessing after the immersion, but a nidda (a woman in the state of menstrual impurity) must recite the blessing before the tevila. So too wrote SA 200:1. There is an additional advantage in this, that the woman says the blessing while still dressed (in the past, where the mikva was dirty, there was a further advantage in this; see Peninei Halakha: Kashrut 31, n. 7).
However, according to the Behag, Rashi, Ra'avan and Sha'arei Dura, in order to make all the laws of immersion uniform, they established that just as a convert recites the blessing after the immersion, and consequently says "concerning immersion" (al ha-tevila) and not "to immerse" (litbol), so should all who immerse act (Ri in Tosafot). Furthermore, since she is about to become pure, it is preferable that she recite the blessing in purity (Ra'avan and Sha'arei Dura). This is similar to the custom of reciting "concerning the washing of the hands" (al netilat yadayim) after the washing (Peninei Halakha: Berakhot 2:13). So too ruled the Rema. In practice, following the Shela, the custom is to satisfy both views and recite the blessing between two immersions. And although the first immersion is valid, since the purification is completed in the second immersion, when the woman immersing emerges from all doubt because her whole body is wet (above, section 5, and so wrote Ḥavot Ya'ir 181), from this standpoint the woman immersing is considered to be reciting the blessing before the immersion. This is just as with the washing of the hands, where one recites the blessing before the drying, with which the purification is completed. And so is the custom of all women of Ashkenazic descent and most women descended from the lands of the East and North Africa (Ḥida in Shiyurei Berakha 200:2; Ḥikrei Lev YD 2:31; Ḥesed La-alafim 200:1; Eretz Ḥayim (Sithon) 200:1; Ben Ish Ḥai Year 2, Shemini 19, and many others). And although it is forbidden to recite a blessing when the private parts are uncovered, according to most poskim, the private parts being within the water are considered covered (Taz 200:3; Shakh 1; Ḥokhmat Adam 121:14; MB 74:16; Kaf Ha-ḥayim 17. And unlike the Derisha and Penei Me'irot). According to many, unlike men, who even when their private parts are covered by water must still take care that there be a separation between the heart and the private parts, women need not separate between their heart and their private parts, since their private parts are concealed below (Orḥot Ḥayim; SA OḤ 74:4; Shakh; Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav; Peninei Halakha: Women's Prayer 10:7). And some say that ideally a woman too should separate between her heart and her private parts when she says words of holiness, by hugging her body with her arms below the heart or over it (Leḥem Ve-simla 200:3; Kaf Ha-ḥayim OḤ 74:17).

sections.body_en:
Many hold that it is good to perform the hair-washing (ḥafifa) and bathing at night, as close as possible to the tevila (She'iltot, Rif, Rambam and Ra'avad). And some say that it is preferable to perform the hair-washing and bathing during the day, for if she washes at night there is a concern that she will hurry in order to come quickly to her husband (Rashi, Rosh). And some were meticulous to combine the two views: they began washing during the day and finished the washing at night, and immediately upon finishing the washing they immersed (SA 199:3). In practice, every woman should choose the place and time in which she can wash her hair and bathe herself calmly and thoroughly. Some prefer to prepare for the tevila at the mikva, and some prefer to do so at home, in which case it is ideally good that they comb their hair a little again before the tevila (SA 199:3). It is fitting for every woman to check how much time a calm and thorough hair-washing and bathing takes her, and from then on to try to devote this length of time to the bathing and hair-washing before the tevila.6

In order for the tevila to be performed in the most excellent manner, the mikva should be filled with water reaching the height of the heart of most women immersing (SA 198:36). For in deeper water there will be women immersing who will be afraid of the water, and in shallower water the women immersing will have to bend too much. However, even when the water is deeper or shallower, as long as the whole body and the hair can enter the water, one may immerse in it.

Ideally, the mikva water is heated so that it will be pleasant for immersion. In addition, in warm water the body is relaxed, and thus the tevila is performed in an excellent manner, with no limb of the body contracted (see above, section 5). However, even when there is no warm water in the mikva, one may ideally immerse in cold water, as Jewish women did for thousands of years.

She should not stand on something that is susceptible to impurity, such as a chair or a stool, and if she immersed while standing on them, her tevila is invalid. For since the immersion must be in the ground and not in a vessel, the Sages decreed that even a woman immersing in a mikva, if she stood on something susceptible to impurity, her tevila is invalid (SA 198:31). So that the woman immersing will not contract her body in a way that might invalidate the tevila, the Sages instructed that she not stand on something from which she might fear she will fall, such as a piece of wood or a brick. However, after the fact (be-di'avad), if she knows that she immersed properly, her tevila is valid (SA 198:31).7

notes_en.en: Some wrote that a woman who postpones the hair-washing to the night should devote a full hour to it, to ensure that she washes her hair and bathes properly (Responsa Maharshal 6; Shakh 199:6). It stands to reason that today, when we have hot running water from the taps and good-quality soap and shampoo, the same hair-washing and bathing can be accomplished in less time. Even in the past there were those who made do with less time. It is also not clear whether the preparations included cutting the nails. Therefore I wrote above in accordance with the fine suggestion of Rav Knohl (Ish Ve-isha, p. 120).

Some say that one should not bathe after the tevila, lest people mistakenly say that the bathing is what can purify, like a mikva (Rokeaḥ; Rema 201:75). However, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim there is no prohibition in this. Some of them did not mention the prohibition (Rif, Rambam, Rosh and others), and some wrote explicitly that there is no prohibition in this (Rid, Maharam of Rothenburg, Mordekhai, Sha'arei Dura, Radbaz 4:205, Gra, Or Same'aḥ). Even according to those who are stringent, the prohibition applies only at the mikva, but at home there is no prohibition to shower (Tzitz Eliezer 11:64; Shulḥan Shlomo by Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach 11:25).

sections.body_en:
Since the woman does not see herself during her tevila, there is reason to be concerned that perhaps one of the hairs of her head remained floating on the surface of the water and her tevila is invalid. Therefore, a responsible woman must stand and see that the whole body and all the hairs of the woman immersing have entered the water (SA 198:40). Since this was so, some were accustomed to ask that same woman also to help them check that there is nothing interposing on their bodies in the places they cannot see. From this the custom developed that in every mikva there is a balanit, who guides new women immersing and helps experienced ones to immerse properly, without interposition.

In practice, there are mikvaot where it is accepted that before the tevila the balanit goes over the required preparations with the woman immersing to make sure she has not forgotten anything, and there are mikvaot where the balanit even helps in examining the body and the nails for any trace of interposition. And there are mikvaot where the balanit only sees that all the hairs have entered the water. The proper approach is that when the woman immersing enters the mikva, while she is still dressed, the balanit should ask what assistance she wants, and should not impose on her assistance that she does not want, because there are women who are very hurt by intervention against their will. In addition, balaniot must refrain from imposing on the women immersing stringencies and pious customs, such as removing well-applied makeup or dye that has no substance (below, section 12), or cutting nails that are well done or removing hard skin on the feet and the like (below, section 13).

A woman who is in a place where there is no woman who can accompany her tevila may immerse alone if her hair is short. And if her hair is long, she should ask her husband to see that during her tevila all her hairs entered the water (Maharam of Rothenburg; Noda Bi-Yehuda Tinyana YD 122). Another option is for her to wrap her hair in a cloth or tie it with a ribbon, taking care that they are loose, and thereby ensure that all her hairs will be within the water (SA 198:40).8

notes_en.en:
It is a pious custom that immediately after her tevila the woman immersing should meet a worthy person, and not an unworthy person or an impure animal (Rema 198:48). Thanks to the presence of the balanit at the mikva, it turns out that all the women immersing fulfill this pious custom (Sha'arei Dura; Likutei Maharil. Some even touch the hand of the balanit, but even according to the pious custom there is no need for this; see Sidrei Tahara 198:91).
The basis of the custom of the balanit: Several Rishonim wrote that another woman must stand and see that all the hairs of the woman immersing are within the water (Rosh). And if there is no woman, she should ask this of her husband (Maharam of Rothenburg, Orḥot Ḥayim). And some added that if she wrapped a cloth around her hair, her tevila counts (Rashba, Meiri, SA 198:40). And some wrote these as two equal options, that she be assisted by her friend or wrap a cloth (Ra'avad). In any event, the custom of the balanit is of great importance, for experience shows that without the presence of a good balanit at the tevila, there are women immersing who err in halakha, and there is no one to correct their error. However, a woman who is embarrassed for a balanit to see her, or who for another reason does not wish to be assisted by a balanit, is not obligated to follow the custom, and she may immerse alone, taking care that all her hair is within the water. First, because there are Rishonim who did not write that another woman must supervise her tevila (Rif, Rambam and others). Second, even those who hold that one should be assisted by a woman agree that if the woman immersing saw to this herself, her tevila counts. However, in a place where the community is particular about the custom of the balanit and wishes to strengthen it as a norm, it may be established that in their mikva one immerses only with a balanit, as is accepted, provided that there is a reasonable solution for a woman who does not wish to immerse with a balanit.

sections.body_en:
The time for a woman's immersion for her purification is after nightfall (tzeit ha-kokhavim) at the conclusion of the shiv'a neki'im (seven clean days): if she began counting the seven clean days on Monday night, then after seven days she immerses on Monday night. In a time of need, it is permitted to immerse a little earlier, during bein ha-shmashot (twilight), that is, in the time between sunset and nightfall.

In a pressing situation, when it is not possible to immerse after nightfall or during bein ha-shmashot, she may immerse earlier, a little before sunset, provided that she does not arrive home before nightfall.

When she cannot immerse even close to sunset, for personal reasons, or because criminals are present in the vicinity of the place of immersion at those hours, or because the cold becomes very severe at night and the woman immersing may catch cold, she should postpone her tevila to the eighth day and immerse during daytime hours (Nidda 67b; SA 197:3-4). However, she should try to conceal this, so that people will not learn from it that one may immerse by day even without great need. She must also take care not to meet with her husband until after nightfall.9

notes_en.en:
The time of a nidda's immersion is after the conclusion of the seven days of nidda, as it is stated (Vayikra 15:19): "She shall be in her separation seven days", which the Sages expounded (Torat Kohanim ad loc.): "She shall be in her separation for all seven", and only after the conclusion of the seven days may she immerse. If she immersed before the end of the seventh day, she remains in her impurity. The Sages instructed that even a woman who postponed her tevila to the eighth day or later should immerse at night, because of "serakh bitah" (lest her daughter learn from her), who might learn from her that it is permitted to immerse on the seventh day (Nidda 67b; SA 197:3).
The time of immersion for other impure people, including a zava, is by day (Yoma 6b; Rambam, Hilkhot Issurei Bi'ah 4:6). That is, by Torah law a zava may immerse on the seventh day, and from the moment of her immersion she is pure and permitted to her husband, even though the seventh day has not yet ended. But if she sees blood before the end of the seventh day, her purity is annulled, and it becomes clear retroactively that the union with her husband took place in violation of a Torah prohibition. Therefore the Sages made a fence around the Torah and forbade a zava to immerse on the seventh day; rather, she should wait until night and immerse. Thus, in practice, the time of immersion is at night, both for a nidda and for a zava.
Today, when all women are considered possible zavot, one must take care that the tevila be on the night after the end of the seventh day, in accordance with the enactment of the Sages. And if she transgressed and immersed on the seventh day, some say that her tevila is invalid (Ra'avad, Maharam and Maharil), but according to most Rishonim her tevila is valid (Rambam, Ramban, Kolbo, Rashba, Ran, Meiri). So too it was ruled in SA 197:4-5. Likewise, a woman who was compelled to postpone her tevila to the eighth day should not immerse by day, according to the Rishonim mentioned, because of "serakh bitah"; and only when, because of circumstances beyond her control, she cannot immerse at night, should she postpone her tevila to the eighth day and immerse by day; and so it was ruled in SA 197:4-5. (However, according to Ra'aviya, Rabbenu Simḥa and Ra'ah, it was only when niddot immersed at the end of the seventh day from the beginning of the veset (menstrual period) that the Sages decreed that she not immerse on the eighth day by day because of "serakh bitah", lest she immerse on the seventh day, when immersion is invalid by Torah law. But today, when the seven clean days are counted, it is permitted to immerse on the eighth day ideally. And according to the Razah it is permitted even on the seventh day ideally, because the rabbinic prohibition against immersing on the seventh day as well applies only to a definite zava.)
According to Rabbenu Tam, Maḥzor Vitry and Sha'arei Dura, when they said that the time of immersion is at night, they meant that the woman should return home from the tevila after dark, even if she immerses on the seventh day. According to the Rashbam, the immersion itself must be at night. And some say that Rabbenu Tam permitted immersing in such a way that she returns home after dark only on the eighth day (Rabbenu Yeruḥam, Tur, and Shakh 197:6).
Some are stringent and rule like the Rashbam, that under no circumstances is immersion on the seventh day to be permitted (Be'er Sheva; Torat Ha-shelamim 197:9; Avnei Nezer YD 250; Da'at Kohen 88). On the other hand, some are lenient on the basis of Rabbenu Tam, that in a pressing situation she may immerse on the seventh day provided that she returns home after dark (Avodat Ha-Gershuni 20; Sidrei Tahara 9; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 14). And some were lenient in this on condition that she cannot reach her home until it gets dark (Ḥatam Sofer YD 197).
In practice, in a time of need one may immerse during bein ha-shmashot, since it is possible that even according to the Rashbam and those who agree with him it is already considered night. And so many women immerse ideally during bein ha-shmashot on Friday night (Taharat Ha-bayit 14:5; Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Shulḥan Shlomo 12:19). In a pressing situation, since the law is rabbinic, one may rely on those who are lenient to immerse before sunset, on condition that she does not meet with her husband until it gets dark. In Igrot Moshe YD 3:60 he added that in a pressing situation she may return home even before it gets dark if the husband has gone to the synagogue and will return only after Ma'ariv, or if there are children in her home who go to sleep only after dark. A woman traveling for Shabbat to her husband who is serving on a military base where there is no mikva should immerse by day and refrain from meeting with him in private until after dark. And if there are children with her, she may meet with him before dark.

sections.title_en: It Is a Mitzva to Become Pure Without Delay
sections.body_en:
It is a mitzva to begin counting the seven clean days as soon as possible, and immediately upon their completion to immerse, in order to fulfill the mitzvot of ona and peru u-revu (procreation), which are two great Torah mitzvot. Without circumstances beyond one's control, it is forbidden to postpone the tevila even one night (SA 197:2). Even on days when a woman cannot become pregnant, such as during pregnancy or nursing, it is forbidden to delay the tevila even by one day, because of the mitzva of ona. All the more so it is forbidden to delay the tevila because of a quarrel; rather, as long as they do not intend to divorce, she is obligated to immerse as soon as possible, and they must do everything to make peace and to fulfill the union with love and joy (Beit Yosef 197:2). Even when it is not possible to fulfill the union because of illness, it is a mitzva to immerse as soon as possible, because there is a mitzva in the other expressions of affection and closeness as well (Maharam of Lublin 53; Shakh 197:3).

Although it is proper for a woman to be discreet about her tevila, the tevila should not be postponed on this account. Even when the couple are guests and the woman cannot conceal her tevila, they should not postpone the tevila without the full agreement of both spouses.10

notes_en.en:
Tanna'im and Rishonim disagreed as to whether there is a mitzva for impure people to immerse as soon as the time for their immersion arrives. According to Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel, Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Meir, it is a mitzva. According to the Sages and Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda, it is not a mitzva (Shabbat 121a; Yoma 8a; Nidda 29b). Some say that the halakha follows those who hold that "immersion at its proper time is a mitzva", and today too it is a mitzva to immerse at the proper time according to the enactment and the custom (She'iltot, Behag, Rabbenu Ḥananel, Razah, Ha-teruma, Semag, Maharik). And some say that both in the past and today immersion at its proper time is not a mitzva (Rabbenu Tam, Ra'aviya, Yere'im and others. And from the Ra'avad and Ha-shlama it is implied that in the past, when they immersed according to Torah law, immersion at its proper time was a mitzva, but today, when the immersion is postponed because of the enactment, immersion at its proper time is not a mitzva. See Peninei Halakha: Yamim Nora'im 9, n. 4, that in practice one does not immerse on Yom Kippur). However, from the standpoint of the mitzvot of ona and peru u-revu, it is a mitzva and a great obligation to immerse early, at the earliest possible time. And although SA 197:2 mentioned only the mitzva of peru u-revu, his intent was to include the mitzva of ona as well, for wherever the poskim wrote about neglecting peru u-revu they also meant neglecting the mitzva of ona; and the proof is that they did not distinguish between a pregnant or nursing woman and one who can become pregnant. This is what the Sages meant when they said (Eruvin 63b) that Yehoshua bin Nun was punished in that he had no sons because he kept Israel from procreation for one night. And so it is explained in Terumat Ha-deshen 255. So too wrote Taz 197:4; Nekudot Ha-kesef ad loc.; Badei Ha-shulḥan 13, Bi'urim ad loc., and many others.
The Sages said in the Zohar (vol. 2, 111a): There are two bad women, for the voice of the impure and harmful serpent can take hold of them. One is she who immerses before the permitted time and has relations with her husband in impurity. The second is she whose time of immersion has arrived and who postpones it in order to cause her husband distress. On the other hand, if the husband caused his wife distress before her tevila, he is obligated to appease her so that she will immerse with joy. In the name of the Arizal it was said that the delay causes evil spirits to descend into the world in place of good souls. See Peninei Halakha: Simḥat Ha-bayit U-virkhato 1:4, n. 4; 8:6, that the mitzva of ona is obligatory even when there is no possibility of pregnancy, and that from this mitzva holy souls flow forth into the world.
Some permitted postponing tevila to the eighth day in order to keep the tevila discreet from neighbors and older children (Kapei Aharon vol. 1, YD 9; Rav Pe'alim vol. 2, YD 33). And one authority permitted a shopkeeper, who, if she closed her shop toward evening, everyone would know that she was immersing, to postpone her tevila to Friday night (Yehuda Ya'aleh YD 217). Responsa Beit She'arim YD 280 rejected his words with strong arguments. It appears that these leniencies were stated for the living conditions of the past, when people lived in great crowding, guarded privacy less, and were more inclined to interfere in other people's lives. However, today, when it has become accepted to guard privacy more, one should not permit postponing tevila out of concern that people will notice it. Therefore, when a couple are guests in the home of relatives, they should not postpone the tevila on this account; and if they wish to postpone it, as long as it is not unavoidable, it is better that they stay at home and not postpone the tevila and the mitzva of ona. Similar to this wrote the Shevet Ha-levi (5:118:2).
Even when the husband is out of town, as long as there is a chance he will return early, it is a mitzva for her to immerse as soon as possible, so that she will be pure when he returns. And so soldiers' wives must take care to do this (and one need not be concerned about the mystical danger (sakana segulit) cited in Shevut Ya'akov 3:77; see Darkhei Tahara 17:4).

sections.body_en:
A woman who must immerse on Friday night should perform the hair-washing, bathing and the other preparations on Friday, at a time when she can perform them calmly, each woman according to her nature and the routine of her life. After completing the preparations she should gather her hair in a way that will keep it free of knots until the tevila. If she performed the main preparations in the morning, she should try to bathe and comb her hair a little again close to Shabbat.

In most communities the custom is to immerse in hot water on Shabbat as well, and although the Sages forbade bathing in hot water on Shabbat, they rely on the opinion of those who hold that this prohibition does not apply to immersion for a mitzva. And in communities where the custom is to take into account the opinion of those who hold that the prohibition of bathing in hot water applies to immersion as well, the tevila is performed in lukewarm water, or during bein ha-shmashot, which is a time when, according to many, it is still permitted to bathe in hot water (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 14:9, n. 8).

A woman immersing on Shabbat must be careful not to wring out her hair in order to speed its drying, but it is permitted to dry it with a towel, and there is no need to be concerned that in doing so she will squeeze water out of her hair, since this squeezing is done incidentally and she has no interest in the water absorbed in the towel (Peninei Halakha: Shabbat 14:8).

In a time of need, the hair-washing may be separated from the tevila by up to two days. Therefore, when the time of the tevila falls on Friday night and on Friday there is a festival on which it is forbidden to wash the hair, the Sages instructed that she wash her hair and bathe on Thursday. Afterward she should gather and tie her hair in a way that it will not tangle, and on Friday night before the tevila she should rinse the places that may have become dirty in the meantime, clean her teeth, examine her whole body and hair to make sure that nothing interposing has stuck to them, and immerse. Likewise, if Rosh Ha-shana falls on Thursday and Friday, she should wash her hair and bathe on Wednesday (Nidda 67b-68a; SA 199:6).11

Some say that a woman who could have immersed and postponed her tevila for various reasons should not immerse on Friday night, for immersion on Friday night was permitted reluctantly for a woman for whom the first night on which she could become pure for her husband is Friday night, but not for one who postponed her tevila for no reason. And although ideally one must be careful not to postpone the tevila to Friday night for no reason, if she did postpone it, she should immerse on Friday night and not postpone her tevila another night.12

notes_en.en: In the past, when it was difficult to arrange the hair-washing on Motza'ei Shabbat (Saturday night), there were poskim who instructed that she wash her hair and bathe well on Friday as well, in preparation for the tevila on Motza'ei Shabbat (Rema 199:4). Today, when all the preparations can be performed on Motza'ei Shabbat with good lighting and hot water, it is enough to perform them on Motza'ei Shabbat.

The Ra'avad forbade immersing on Friday night out of concern about wringing out the hair. On the other hand, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim, one may immerse on Friday night even an immersion that could have been performed earlier. And so is the custom of those of Sephardic and Eastern descent (Beit Yosef 197:2; Taharat Ha-bayit 14:3). However, in many communities in Ashkenaz a custom was widespread not to perform on Friday night an immersion that could have been performed earlier, because of concern about wringing and carrying (Maharil Ḥadashot 96; Mahari Weil, Piskei 48), and because they were not accustomed to bathe in cold water, and consequently her immersion looked like an act of improvement (tikkun) (Terumat Ha-deshen 255-256, based on Beitza 17b). So too is the opinion of the Baḥ and Taz 4. According to Rema 197:2, in a place where they were not accustomed to be stringent, one should not be stringent. So too wrote Shakh 3; Torat Ha-shelamim 5; Ḥokhmat Adam 118:8. In practice, the custom spread throughout all the communities of Ashkenaz to immerse on Friday night even an immersion that had been postponed (Olat Shabbat OḤ 326:15-16; Ba'er Heitev 5; Responsa of Rabbi Eliyahu Guttmacher vol. 1, YD 54; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 197:8).

sections.body_en:
The general rules of the laws of interposition were explained in section 2; from here to the end of the chapter we will deal with the details of the laws of interposition.

An interposition that invalidates the tevila is something that adheres to the body or the hair and that one is particular to remove; for example, one is embarrassed by it and is therefore particular to remove it when going out into the street. But things that a woman wants to be attached to her body are subordinate to the body and considered part of it, and therefore they do not interpose. Accordingly, eye and face makeup, foundation cream for the face and lipstick do not interpose, provided that they are well applied and will remain intact even after the tevila. But if they have become damaged, or will become damaged during the tevila, in a way that she or most women are particular to remove them, they interpose.

Nail polish, gel polish or a build-up on the nails, as long as they are intact, do not interpose. But if they were damaged in a way that she or most women are particular to remove and repair them, they interpose (long nails are discussed in the next section).

Rings, earrings and nose rings that are attached tightly to the body, if there is no time at which the woman is particular to remove them, do not interpose (Tashbetz 3:280); and if the woman is particular to remove them, such as a decorated ring that the woman is particular to remove whenever she kneads dough and prepares food with her hands, or earrings that she is particular to remove whenever she bathes, then since there is no fixed time at which she wants them to be on her, they interpose.13

Dye that has no substance, such as ink, henna and hair dye, since it has no substance, does not interpose even when one does not want it. Similarly, hand cream and body cream, even when their oiliness can be felt, since they have no substance, do not interpose. However, when possible, meticulous women are accustomed ideally to immerse without cream and to remove dye that has no substance.

Paint that has substance, that is, which can be felt to the touch, interposes. But if the woman's occupation is painting, her law is like that of people who work with paint, for whom stains that they are not particular to remove do not interpose (SA 198:17). However, when it is not difficult, the custom is to be meticulous and remove them.

notes_en.en:
The Rishonim wrote that makeup colors do not interpose because something intended for beauty does not interpose, and furthermore, because something that has no substance does not interpose (Ramban, Rashba, Rosh, Rabbenu Yeruḥam, Meiri, Ritva, Orḥot Ḥayim and others). The Baḥ held that the main leniency is for color that has no substance, but if it has substance, then even when she wants it, it interposes; and he learned this from Nidda 67a, that eye-shadow (kohl) outside the eye interposes. However, the overwhelming majority of the Aḥaronim disagreed with him and hold that even color that has substance does not interpose if the woman wants it (Binat Adam 12:21; Ohel Yosef 40; MB 161:12, and BHL s.v. "ve-hayu"; Igrot Moshe YD 3:62, and many others). Some argue that since women are particular to remove makeup from time to time so that the skin can breathe, makeup interposes like a ring that one usually removes. However, there is a difference between them: the ring she will remove at any hour of the day at which she needs to knead or prepare food with her hands, so that there is no set time during which she is particular that the ring be on her. Whereas with makeup, throughout the time she wants it to be on her she will never want to remove it, so that during that time it is subordinate to the body and does not interpose (Penei Arye 6; Igrot Moshe YD 1:97). It should further be added that makeup clings to the body and is therefore more subordinate to it, whereas rings and earrings are not so subordinate to the body, and therefore whenever she usually removes them at times, they are no longer considered subordinate to the body. It must also be added that in the past women were accustomed every day to knead dough and prepare food with their hands, and removing rings was frequent; but today, when the woman removes them only rarely, while kneading, there is room to say that they are subordinate to the body. However, in practice, since the custom has already been to consider a ring that she removes for kneading as interposing, even though this has become rare, one should continue the custom of considering it interposing. But what one is not accustomed to remove does not interpose. And although many women are meticulous to remove even things that do not interpose, including makeup, as the Rema wrote (198:1), nevertheless, when there is a great need, such as makeup in honor of Shabbat, one may ideally immerse with the makeup (as explained above at the end of n. 1).
Tight earrings and nose rings that she never removes do not interpose (Meiri, Nidda 66b; Tashbetz 3:280; see Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, p. 116). And so wrote Gan Ha-melekh 123 regarding a ring for netilat yadayim (washing of the hands), that one whose work is clean and who never removes his ring need not remove it. And so is the opinion of the Maharshal, Eliyahu Rabba, and MB 161:19. And so they learned for the law of women's immersion (Ḥokhmat Adam 119:4; Ikarei Ha-Dat, and many others, as cited in Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, pp. 111-113). However, some hold that even a tight ring that she is not accustomed to remove interposes (Sidrei Tahara 198:44; Leḥem Ve-simla 56; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 52). But the main halakhic ruling is that a woman who never removes her ring need not remove it for the tevila, since this is the opinion of most poskim, and in addition the law is rabbinic. A woman who is particular to remove her ring while kneading, but whose finger has widened or swelled so that she cannot remove it: since in practice the ring is on her finger permanently, it does not interpose (Tzitz Eliezer 20:26). And it is good that after she enters the water she turn her ring so that water will get under it, and thus her tevila will be valid even according to the stringent view (Be-ohala shel Torah vol. 1, YD 28).

sections.title_en: Nails and Things Attached to the Body
sections.body_en:
Long nails do not interpose, since they are part of the body; but if there is dirt stuck to them that women are particular to remove, even if it is small, it interposes. Therefore women were accustomed to cut their nails before the tevila, lest dirt be stuck to them. However, women who wish to grow their nails need not cut them, but only see to it that they are clean.14

A wart on the body, even if it has begun to come away, does not interpose, since it is still part of the body (Semag). Likewise, strips of skin next to the nail (hangnails), and peeling skin, such as skin burned by the sun, do not interpose. Hard, dry skin on the sole of the foot does not interpose. Regarding all these, when they can be removed without difficulty, meticulous women are accustomed ideally to remove them (see Rema 198:22, and Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, p. 78).

notes_en.en:
Dirt under the nail that one is particular to remove interposes, and in order to remove the doubt the custom was to cut the nails before the tevila (see Tosefta Mikva'ot 6:10; Rashba; SA 198:18, 20). According to the Ra'avan, nails that are about to be cut interpose even though there is no dirt in them (and Shakh 198:25 took his view into account). However, according to the overwhelming majority of the Rishonim and Aḥaronim, long nails do not interpose in any case (Teruma, Ra'aviya, Mordekhai, Sha'arei Dura and others). The Rema (198:20) was indeed stringent that if she did not cut even one nail, she must immerse again. However, this stringency is in order to preserve the custom and not because there really is an interposition in this (Taz 21; Maharam of Lublin 71; Torat Ha-shelamim, Sidrei Tahara, Leḥem Ve-simla, Responsa Mitzpeh Arye Tinyana YD 35). In recent generations women began to grow their nails long for beauty, and many were stringent and instructed that they be removed, in order to preserve the custom, and also because it is not fitting to be drawn after new fashions. But they agreed that if because of this the woman will not want to immerse, it is better that she immerse with long nails (Aḥiezer 3:33; Mishpetei Uziel vol. 2, YD 32; Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, p. 98).
In practice, a woman who wishes to grow her nails long for beauty may immerse with them, because according to all opinions they do not interpose, for even according to the Ra'avan only a nail that is about to be cut interposes, and here it is not about to be cut (Responsa Hillel Omer YD 96; Tevu'at Shemesh YD 53; Ve-zot Li-Yehuda YD 22). And it appears that even those inclined to be stringent about this in the past were stringent in a place and time in which nearly all women were accustomed to cut their nails. However, in a place where many women, including religious women, are accustomed to grow their nails long for beauty, it is permitted ideally to immerse with long nails, and even with a build-up and polish on them, provided that the polish or build-up is attractive. It further appears according to this that today, even a woman who is accustomed to cut her nails in preparation for the tevila, if she forgot to cut them and immersed, need not immerse again. And it stands to reason that even the Rema would agree to this. All the more so, a woman who forgot to cut her nails on Friday night should not refrain from immersing, but should take care that they be clean.

sections.body_en:
Blood and pus that have dried on a wound, if they are in a state in which one usually leaves them, because it hurts to remove them or so as not to interfere with the healing of the wound, are part of the body and do not interpose. But if they are in a state in which one usually removes them, such as a scab outside the wound, they interpose. In any event, any woman who bathes herself well in hot water before the tevila need not be concerned about the scabs on her, for the hot water removes everything that one is usually particular about.15

Similarly, a bandage and a plaster, or a thick ointment on a wound, which she is careful not to remove, either because it hurts to remove them or because removing them harms the healing, do not interpose. And if removing them involves no pain or harm, they interpose.16

Stitches after surgery or a cut do not interpose, since one wants them to remain for the sake of recovery. And from the time that, medically, they can be taken out, if they are unsightly or uncomfortable, they interpose. Dissolving stitches do not interpose in any case.

A splinter lodged in the flesh, if it is entirely embedded in the flesh, even though it is very bothersome, does not interpose. And if its upper end protrudes, since it is bothersome and she wants to remove it, it interposes (SA 198:11). And if she tried to take it out and did not succeed, then against her will it has become subordinate to her flesh and does not interpose.

A woman who has a cast on her arm or leg, if it is difficult to remove it because this may harm the healing or because of the great effort involved, since she wants it to remain on her, it does not interpose. If it is a cast with which one can immerse, she should immerse with it. And if it is a cast that will be damaged by water, she should wrap it in plastic and stick the edges of the plastic to her flesh in a way that ensures the cast does not get wet, and immerse with it, so that the mikva water will surround all of her together with the cast. Admittedly, some are stringent about this, because an ordinary woman does not want a cast to be on her body, and she needs it only because of the injury. However, since in practice she needs the cast, she now wants it, and consequently it does not interpose. In addition, as long as the cast is not on most of the body, even according to the stringent view the interposition is rabbinic. Furthermore, being stringent about this harms the Torah mitzva of ona. Therefore one should rule according to the lenient view.17

notes_en.en: Some hold that no scab interposes, since it is attached to the body (Ra'avad; see Shakh 198:13). On the other hand, some are inclined to be stringent and remove even scabs that one generally does not usually remove (Derashot Maharaḥ Or Zaru'a 22; Darkhei Tahara 16:44-45). And the opinion of most Rishonim is that any scab whose removal involves pain does not interpose, since she does not want to remove it (Ramban, Rashba, Semag, Semak, Ha-teruma, Mordekhai and others). In any event, when one washes the area in hot water, the scab that one usually removes comes off or softens in a way that, according to all opinions, there is no interposition in it (Rosh, Tur and SA 198:9). Therefore, today, when it is easy to wash the whole body well in hot water, this is the proper guidance in order to remove all doubt.

Admittedly, some hold that even when removing the bandage is painful, as long as there is no danger or terrible pain involved, one must remove it (Teshuva Me-ahava 3:198:10; Binat Adam, Beit Ha-nashim 12; Tzemaḥ Tzedek YD 158). On the other hand, many are lenient even when removing the bandage involves pain or slight harm, since she is careful not to remove it (Rabbi Akiva Eiger 4:55; Divrei Ḥayim 2:68; Rav Pe'alim vol. 2, YD 28; Yad Sofer 35). And since according to the rules of interposition the main view is that of the lenient, and in addition the dispute concerns a rabbinic law, the halakha is to be lenient.

Some are stringent that even if the cast will be on the woman for a long time, she should not immerse until it is removed (Mishpetei Uziel vol. 9, YD 26; Ḥut Shani 198:31; Mishmeret Ha-tahara 198:85, in the name of Rav Yosef Shalom Elyashiv). Their opinion relies on the words of SA 198:10, that a dressing (retiya) on the body interposes. This is because an ordinary person is particular that there be no bandage or cast on his body, and furthermore, perhaps the cast was made larger than medically necessary. However, if there is a concern that as a result of delaying the purification they will come to a transgression, or even to sinful thoughts, one should be lenient (Har Tzvi YD 165). On the other hand, the simple reasoning is that anyone who needs a cast for his healing is not particular about it, as is evident from the fact that he walks around with it in the street. So too wrote Tzitz Eliezer 4:9; Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, p. 57, and Rav Rabinovitch. And there is no room to be stringent about this, because of the harm to the Torah mitzva of ona. Women who wish to be meticulous will find ways to remove the cast before the tevila and put it back immediately afterward.

sections.body_en:
A piece of meat or bone lodged between the teeth interposes, for we have learned (section 3) that with hidden places that are sometimes exposed, although there is no need for the mikva water to come into contact with them, there must be no interposition in them. Therefore, out of concern that a piece of meat may remain lodged between the teeth, many women were accustomed not to eat meat on the day of their tevila (SA 198:24). Today, when we have dental floss, a woman who knows how to clean all her teeth with it need not refrain from eating meat on the day of the tevila.

Dental fillings, permanent and even temporary, as well as an appliance glued to the teeth to straighten them (braces), do not interpose, since one wants them to remain. Dentures do not interpose.18

Contact lenses do not interpose, since they are not tight against the eye. However, since some hold that they interpose, it is ideally proper to remove them.19

A vaginal ring for contraception does not interpose. A contraceptive patch should be removed, but after the fact, if she did not remove it, it does not interpose.20

A woman who suffers from an ear disease, and on the doctor's instructions is forbidden to get her ears wet for fear of infection, should seal her ears according to his guidance and immerse that way. However, when possible it is proper for her to turn to a God-fearing doctor, so that the medical guidance will be as medically necessary and no more.21

notes_en.en:
Some were stringent about a temporary filling, since the woman immersing was compelled to have it put in because of circumstances beyond her control, and only if it was put in for a month has it become part of the tooth and does not interpose (Badei Ha-shulḥan 198:179). And some were stringent if it was put in for less than a week (Rav Shlomo Zalman Auerbach in Shulḥan Shlomo 10:13-14). However, according to many it does not interpose, for a person who needs a filling wants it, and on the contrary, is careful not to remove it until the end of the treatment (Imrei Esh YD 75-76; Sho'el U-meshiv Tinyana 3:108; Mishpetei Uziel vol. 9, YD 28; Igrot Moshe YD 1:97). In addition, according to many, the law of interposition in hidden places is rabbinic. Furthermore, the interposition is only on a minority of the body, whose prohibition is rabbinic. Therefore one should be lenient. It should be added that perhaps some of those who were stringent in the past were stringent because fillings were unsightly and some were embarrassed to go out with them; but today there is no embarrassment at all in temporary fillings. Stitches in the gums do not interpose, since she wants them (Dovev Meisharim 3:40; Orot Ha-tahara 13:62).
Dentures: Some are stringent that they interpose, since one is sometimes accustomed to remove them (Maharsham 1:78). And many hold that they do not interpose, since women want them, like makeup, and in addition, one can also sleep with them (Rav Pe'alim vol. 4, YD 13; Shulḥan Shlomo 10:21; Orot Ha-tahara 13:61). And since the law is rabbinic on two counts, the halakha follows the lenient view.

Some say that contact lenses interpose even after the fact, since one is particular to remove them before sleep (Minḥat Yitzḥak 6:89; Darkhei Tahara 16:21). And some say that they do not interpose, since they are not fastened tightly to the eye but there is moisture between them; however, ideally one should remove them (Igrot Moshe YD 1:104; Beit Avi 1:101; Si'aḥ Naḥum 62). In practice, since this concerns "beit ha-setarim", in which according to many the interposition is rabbinic, and it is a minority of the body, the doubt here is rabbinic on two counts, and the halakha follows the lenient view. However, ideally, since there are those who are stringent, when it is not difficult it is proper to take their view into account. A prosthetic eye that she is embarrassed to remove does not interpose (Har Tzvi YD 161).

A vaginal ring for contraception (NuvaRing) does not interpose, because it is not tightly attached and there is natural moisture beneath it (Si'aḥ Naḥum 61). In addition, it appears that the inside of the vagina is not "beit ha-setarim" but rather like the internal places of the body, in which there is no law of interposition. Admittedly, some are inclined to be stringent and remove it (Darkhei Tahara 16:80. In Responsa Puah, Contraception, p. 128, the opinions of rabbis both lenient and stringent are cited). However, since it is a rabbinic doubt on two counts, and the reasoning of the lenient view seems very compelling, one should permit it ideally. A patch for contraception or for pain: some say that it interposes, since it is on the body and not in "beit ha-setarim", and the woman does not want to be seen with it (Puah vol. 1, 19:54). On the other hand, there is room to say that since she wants it to remain for a period of time, its law is like that of a bandage, which does not interpose (above, n. 17). In practice, since many are stringent, it should be removed. However, after the fact, since it is a rabbinic doubt and the reasoning of the lenient view is plausible, her tevila counts.

Some poskim wrote that the solution is to insert cotton wool deep into the ear, so that it may perhaps be considered an internal place in which there is no interposition, or at least be considered "beit ha-setarim", in which according to many the laws of interposition are rabbinic (see Emek She'ela YD 46; Taharat Ha-bayit vol. 3, pp. 63-72; Igrot Moshe YD 1:98-103). And some raised various solutions for various medical conditions, such as, for example, that she go about with the cotton wool for two days or a week (see Darkhei Tahara 16:23; Tzitz Eliezer 5:31; Orot Ha-tahara 13:57). However, there is strong reasoning to be lenient: since the woman wants the sealing in order to prevent a risk to the ear, the law of the sealing is like that of a bandage (above, n. 16). And although she wants it only at the time of contact with the water, nevertheless at that time she wants it very much. So too wrote Rav Meir Arik in Imrei Yosher 2:82; and see Tzitz Eliezer 5:31; 4:9:3. And since it is a rabbinic doubt on two counts, for the interposition is on part of the body, and the ear is "beit ha-setarim", the halakha is to be lenient. If there were no risk in this, there would be room to take into account the stringent view; but since experience shows that there is a risk of serious ear disease in this, there is no room to be stringent. Therefore, one should instruct her to seal the ear according to the doctor's instructions and immerse. However, when possible, it is proper to go to a God-fearing doctor, for there are situations in which, instead of sealing the ear, it can be disinfected with antibiotic drops after the tevila, or substances can be used that can protect the ear without interposition. Even a doctor who does not wear a kippa but treats the Torah with respect and takes an interest in the instructions of halakha in order to help his patients is considered God-fearing. However, in practice, even a woman who went to a doctor who is not God-fearing, since she seals her ear according to medical instruction, the law of the sealing is like that of a bandage, which does not interpose.

sections.body_en:
As we have learned (in section 2), there is special importance to immersing the hair together with the body, to the point that the hair is equivalent to the body; and just as an interposition on most of the body that she is particular to remove invalidates the tevila by Torah law, so an interposition on most of the hair that she is particular to remove invalidates the tevila by Torah law. And as with the body, an interposition on a minority of the hair that one is particular to remove interposes by rabbinic law. Therefore, if glue or some filth that women are usually particular to remove, or that she is accustomed to remove, was stuck to the hair, it interposes.

If there were knots in her hair: if the knot is of two hairs together, it stands to reason that it is not so tight and the water enters it, and therefore it does not interpose even if she is particular to remove such knots. But if the knot is of a single hair on itself or on another hair, the water does not enter the place of the knot, and if the number of hairs knotted in this way is of an amount that she is particular about, or that most women are usually particular about, it interposes (SA 198:5).22

A woman who suffers from lice and nits in her hair should wash her head with suitable substances, as is customary, and comb her hair with a suitable comb; and if afterward lice and nits remain in her hair, they do not interpose. For women who do not succeed in removing them with the customary washing and cleaning are compelled, having no choice, not to be particular about them.

Hair extensions that have been tied or glued to the hair of the head or to the eyelashes, with the intention that they remain as long as possible, since the woman wants them, do not interpose.

Braids, thick and even very thin, do not interpose, since the braiding of the braid is not tight, provided that she takes care not to tie the braid with a tight elastic band.

Dreadlocks in the hair interpose, for the hairs in the dreadlocks stick to one another by means of knots and natural oil or added oil, so that there is an interposition on most of the hair. In addition, most women are particular that there be no such interposition in their hair. However, a woman who very much wishes to keep the dreadlocks for the sake of beauty may rely on the opinion of the lenient and immerse with the dreadlocks.23

notes_en.en:
According to the Rambam (Hilkhot Mikva'ot 2:15) and the Meiri, the hair is assessed together with the whole body, and only if there is an interposition that she is particular about on most of the body and hair together does it interpose by Torah law. However, according to the Ge'onim, Rashi, Ra'avad, Rosh, Ran, Tur and SA 198:5, most of the body is assessed separately and most of the hair separately. According to the Rashba, a knot of two hairs interposes, but in practice it was ruled in the Rambam and SA 198:5 that it does not interpose.
Some say that most of the hair means literally most of the area of all the hairs together, and therefore one knot in each of the hairs is not a majority (Avnei Nezer 263:4; Tiferet Tzvi 9:5). And some say that every hair that has a knot is considered a hair that has an interposition, and if most of the hairs have a knot, the interposition is by Torah law (Penei Me'irot 2:147, and Ḥokhmat Adam 119:5). Some say that each collection of hair on the body is assessed on its own (Tiferet Le-Moshe; Arukh Ha-shulḥan 198:25). And some say that all the hair on the body is assessed as one, and one should add to this the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that all the hair is assessed together with the body (Pardes Rimonim; Imrei Yosher 1:197; Rabbi Tzadok in Tiferet Tzvi 9:6, and others).

Most women are particular about this, and as a rule we follow the majority, in accordance with the opinion of the Rashba and SA 198:1, as explained above in n. 1. All the more so, since perhaps with dreadlocks there is an interposition on most of the hair, and according to most Rishonim an interposition on most of the hair that she is particular about interposes by Torah law. However, a woman who very much wants dreadlocks for the sake of beauty may rely on the opinion of the Rambam, who holds that being particular is determined according to the woman, and consequently, since she wants the dreadlocks, there is no interposition in this for her. In addition, according to the Rambam the hair is assessed together with the body, and consequently there is no doubt involving a Torah law. Thus, according to the Rambam, a woman who wishes to keep the dreadlocks may immerse with them. And see Ish Ve-isha by Rav Knohl, p. 116; Rav Yosef Tzvi Rimon (Puah vol. 1, 19, n. 38), and Rav Adiel Assayag (Teḥumin 37). Admittedly, there is room to argue that even according to the Rambam's view, that one follows most of the body and hair together, one should be stringent. For the surface area of the hair, when each hair is counted on its own, can be several times the area of the whole body. And if on a significant majority of the area of the hairs there is an interposition because of the dreadlocks, then even when she is not particular about it, according to the Rambam the interposition invalidates the tevila by rabbinic law. However, one can answer that an interposition on most of the body and hair interposes even when she is not particular about the interposition but also does not want it; but in a case where she wants the interposition, because in her opinion it makes her beautiful, it does not interpose. And perhaps one can even apply this reasoning to the Rashba and SA, who follow the majority of women when the majority is particular and the minority is not particular but also does not want it; but when the minority wants it for the sake of beauty, the opinion of the minority is not nullified by the majority. This is especially so when the matter concerns a minority group, similar to people who work with paint, whose law differs from that of other people (above, end of section 12).
